content.title: Paper positioning, contributions, and acknowledgement of things needing improvement.
content.comment:
We thank all three reviewers for providing valuable feedback on this work and agreeing that:
- It provides a valuable benchmark for deep learning-based 2D-3D reconstruction from X-ray.
- It presents solid experiments with extensive quantitative experiments. 

One of the major concerns reviewers raised is about the novelty. We would like to emphasize, which R-c6kn also rightly pointed out, that as a benchmark paper, our aim is not to provide technical novelty. We believe that works that bring a wide range of datasets into a single standardized format and provide a platform for the community to access them easily, implement others’ works that are non-trivial due to lack of reproducibility, and provide a benchmark for others to build upon are important contributions. The community has realized the importance of benchmarking; for instance, the Neurips conference recently started a dedicated track for such papers. 

Another question raised is about what we can learn from this study. Before this work, it was unclear which of the four primary methods proposed in the literature is better as they have been compared in different datasets with very different setups. Our results show that the approach taken by Kasten et al. and Bayat et al’s are the best compared to others. But we agree that there remains further detailed analysis and insights to be drawn from the experiments that are currently lacking. 

We agree that adding more methods, including the ones that use anatomical priors, would be interesting. Similarly, more extensive ablation studies to identify the influences of CNN architecture, loss, and feature fusion would also be interesting. However, we believe that our work is the first step which is already important and substantial before we go into the suggested work in the future. We have revised the Introduction section to highlight the major problem we see in the current literature, which has three components: i) lack of easy access to dispersed datasets in a standardized form, ii) lack of examples with comprehensive disaggregated reporting of the reports to provide insights on how various domain shifts common in clinical settings impact the results, and iii) most work focus on optimizing methods on commonly used metrics such as Dice Score, but clinical applications for which the methods are intended to be used have clinical parameters which are more important to be optimized for. We have brought together these issues together into a single platform and intend to make it open source. This will enable us (and the community) to work on the kind of work suggested in the review. 

Having said this, we know that our discussion and presentation of already carried out experiments needs some improvement, for which we, unfortunately, could not dedicate enough time during the rebuttal period. Hence, we are withdrawing the paper but would like to thank the reviewers for taking their time to help us improve the paper and submit it to another place.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
In this paper, the 2D xray to 3D CT reconstruction problem is studied. The major contributions are: 
(1) Multiple encoder-decoder based end-to-end architectures are evaluated with the same pre-processing and on the same dataset. 
(2) Provide comprehensive/standardized framework for pre-processing, baseline comparison, and using a set of metrics like Dice, HD and ASD to measure the reconstruction accuracy.
(3) Categories for disagreement reports.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strength
- In this paper, major advances in this area are examined with the same processing protocols, same datasets and same metrics, which provides a standard benchmark for Xray-CT reconstruction task.

### Weakness
- Novelty is limited. This is an experiment-heavy and application heavy work. It's solid in terms of experiments. However, there are no new scientific findings discussed in this work. 
- Benchmark is limited to encoder-decoder and retrieval based methods.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: This paper is clear and easy to follow, authors are committed to make the work open-source.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, this is a solid experiment report, which build a standard and reproducible benchmark system for 2D Xray to 3D CT reconstruction task. However, it also suffered from limitations in scope and novelty.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper presents a thorough analysis and benchmarking of four different 2D to 3D reconstruction methods for estimating 3D bone shapes (segmentations) from two (orthogonal) x-rays. The corresponding pairs of images are simulated using digitally reconstructed radiographs (DRR). The methods are carefully evaluated on a number of different anatomical sites and with varying challenges (pathology, metal artefacts). The authors present re-implementations based on published methods and slightly optimise the hyperparameter choices, in addition they present two retrieval both baselines (lower and upper bounds)
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths**
- The paper very nicely addresses the often problematic issue of reproducible research, it excels at extending previous published work to a common and more comprehensive evaluation setting and provides a very interesting analysis also wrt to domain shifts.
- The article is very well written and carefully explains the adoption steps necessary to make the re-implementations comparable.
- The quantitative results are extensive

**Weaknesses**
- my major concern, aside from obviously missing technical novelty (which isn't the focus of a benchmark paper) is the question of what exactly we can learn from this study? 1) The experiments are restricted to Encoder-Decoder based Architectures while it is mentioned that methods which combine DL and anatomical priors are starting to emerge. Why are those left out? 2) The differences across the four methods mainly revolve around the stage of feature fusion and loss terms. But there are also numerous architectural design choices of the underlying CNN networks. 
- in my opinion it would be necessary to better disentangle the complementary influences of CNN architecture, loss and feature fusion. Ideally by generating a comprehensive meta-framework that has each published work as sub-instance, but can also pave ways for potential improvements.
- a few minor issues: is there a way to quantify the (potential) performance gap in replicating those models on their original respective data sets?, 5.3 IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS doesn't seem to follow common punctuation or capitalisation.
- judging from the visual results in Fig 1, including a combination of DL reconstruction, NN-retrieval and registration should yield very competitive results that should fix many errors of the Shiode and Chen method
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Overall the paper is very clear apart from some minor punctuation errors. The novelty does not lie in a technical contribution but by comparing several published algorithm in a fair setting. While this can yield high praise in terms of reproducibility, the discussion on individually contributing factors of those competing methods falls short.
content.summary_of_the_review: While I really enjoyed reading the paper, I think the limited empirical insight make it unacceptable for a mainly technical machine learning oriented conference, where the medical imaging application is a rather small part. I would recommend the authors to extend the discussion and in-depth comparisons (as outlined above) and submit their work to MIDL or MICCAI.

content.title: Benchmarking Encoder-Decoder Architectures for Biplanar X-ray to 3D Bone Shape Reconstruction
content.abstract:
Various deep learning pipelines have been proposed for 3D Bone Shape Reconstruction from Biplanar X-rays. Although these methods individually report excellent results, we do not know how these architecture pipelines compare against each other since they are reported on different anatomy, datasets, and cohort distribution. We benchmark these disparate architectures on equal footing on three different anatomies using public datasets. We describe various benchmarking tasks to simulate real-world clinical scenarios including reconstruction of fractured bones, bones with implants, robustness to population shift, and estimate clinical parameters. 

We provide an open-source implementation of SOTA architectures, dataset pipelines, and extraction of clinical parameters. 
Comparing the encoder-decoder architectures with baseline retrieval models, we find that the encoder-decoder methods are able to learn from data and are much better than retrieval baselines. However, the best methods have limited difference on performance, but the domain shift plays an important role in deteriorating the performance of these methods.
